summary.text: For each prime \(q\), counting pairs divisible by \(q^i\) gives the numerator valuation \(\sum_i\lfloor N/q^i\rfloor^2\), while Legendre’s formula gives the denominator valuation \(\sum_i\sum_k k\lfloor N/(kq^i)\rfloor\); the bound \(\sum_{k\le M}k\lfloor M/k\rfloor\le M^2\) proves the quotient is exact. If \(p\nmid m+1\), adjoining \(m+1\) adds no \(p\)-factor to any new gcd and leaves every factorial valuation unchanged because \(\lfloor(m+1)/(kp^i)\rfloor=\lfloor m/(kp^i)\rfloor\); iterating this from \(np\) through \(np+p-1\) yields the result.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
N(t)=\prod_{1\le j\le t}\prod_{1\le k\le t}\gcd(j,k),
\qquad
D(t)=\prod_{1\le k\le t}\left(\left\lfloor\frac tk\right\rfloor!\right)^k,
\]
and define
\[
a(t)=\frac{N(t)}{D(t)}.
\]
We will first prove that this quotient is an integer. We then prove a one-step invariance result for its \(p\)-adic order, and finally iterate that result through the interval from \(np\) to \(np+p-1\).

For a prime \(q\), write \(\nu_q(x)\) for the exponent of \(q\) in the prime factorization of a positive integer \(x\). We use the standard facts
\[
\nu_q(xy)=\nu_q(x)+\nu_q(y),\qquad
\nu_q(x^r)=r\nu_q(x),
\]
\[
\nu_q(\gcd(x,y))=\min(\nu_q(x),\nu_q(y)),
\]
and Legendre's formula
\[
\nu_q(s!)=\sum_{i\ge 1}\left\lfloor\frac{s}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
All the displayed infinite sums have only finitely many nonzero terms.

We first establish the divisibility
\[
D(t)\mid N(t)                                                     \tag{1}
\]
for every nonnegative integer \(t\). If \(t=0\), both products are empty and hence equal to \(1\), so there is nothing to prove. Suppose now that \(t>0\), and fix an arbitrary prime \(q\).

By additivity of valuations over products and Legendre's formula,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nu_q(D(t))
&=\sum_{k=1}^t k\,\nu_q\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac tk\right\rfloor!\right)\\
&=\sum_{k=1}^t k\sum_{i\ge1}
   \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor t/k\rfloor}{q^i}\right\rfloor\\
&=\sum_{i\ge1}\sum_{k=1}^t
   k\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor t/k\rfloor}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
                                                               \tag{2}
\end{aligned}
\]
Integer division is associative in the following sense:
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor x/u\rfloor}{v}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{x}{uv}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor x/v\rfloor}{u}\right\rfloor.
\]
Thus, if
\[
M_i=\left\lfloor\frac{t}{q^i}\right\rfloor,
\]
then the inner sum in (2) is
\[
\sum_{k=1}^t k\left\lfloor\frac{M_i}{k}\right\rfloor.
\]
Terms with \(k>M_i\) vanish. For every \(1\le k\le M_i\),
\[
k\left\lfloor\frac{M_i}{k}\right\rfloor\le M_i.
\]
There are \(M_i\) possible values of \(k\) in this range, so
\[
\sum_{k=1}^t k\left\lfloor\frac{M_i}{k}\right\rfloor
=
\sum_{k=1}^{M_i} k\left\lfloor\frac{M_i}{k}\right\rfloor
\le M_i^2.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\nu_q(D(t))\le
\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{t}{q^i}\right\rfloor^2.       \tag{3}
\]

We now compute the valuation of the numerator. Since
\(\nu_q(\gcd(j,k))=\min(\nu_q(j),\nu_q(k))\), we have
\[
\nu_q(N(t))=
\sum_{j=1}^t\sum_{k=1}^t
\min(\nu_q(j),\nu_q(k)).                                      \tag{4}
\]
For any two positive integers \(j,k\),
\[
\min(\nu_q(j),\nu_q(k))
=
\sum_{i\ge1}{\bf 1}_{q^i\mid j\,\text{ and }\,q^i\mid k},    \tag{5}
\]
because the summand is \(1\) precisely for
\(i=1,\ldots,\min(\nu_q(j),\nu_q(k))\). Substituting (5) into
(4) and interchanging the finite sums gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nu_q(N(t))
&=\sum_{i\ge1}
 \#\{(j,k):1\le j,k\le t,\ q^i\mid j,\ q^i\mid k\}\\
&=\sum_{i\ge1}
 \left(\#\{j:1\le j\le t,\ q^i\mid j\}\right)^2\\
&=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{t}{q^i}\right\rfloor^2.    \tag{6}
\end{aligned}
\]
Indeed, the multiples of \(q^i\) between \(1\) and \(t\) are
\(q^i,2q^i,\ldots,\lfloor t/q^i\rfloor q^i\).

Equations (3) and (6) show that
\[
\nu_q(D(t))\le \nu_q(N(t))
\]
for every prime \(q\). Both \(D(t)\) and \(N(t)\) are positive. By unique prime factorization, the primewise valuation inequalities imply (1). Thus \(a(t)=N(t)/D(t)\) is indeed a positive integer, and for every prime \(p\),
\[
\nu_p(a(t))=\nu_p(N(t))-\nu_p(D(t)).                            \tag{7}
\]

We next prove the central one-step assertion:

**One-step assertion.** If \(p\) is prime and \(p\nmid m+1\), then
\[
\nu_p(a(m+1))=\nu_p(a(m)).                                    \tag{8}
\]

We prove separately that the numerator and denominator valuations do not change.

First consider the numerator. Passing from \(N(m)\) to \(N(m+1)\) retains all factors \(\gcd(j,k)\) with \(1\le j,k\le m\), and adds the new row and column in which at least one index is \(m+1\). Every new factor is therefore of one of the forms
\[
\gcd(m+1,k),\qquad \gcd(j,m+1),
\]
including \(\gcd(m+1,m+1)=m+1\). Each such gcd divides \(m+1\). Since \(p\nmid m+1\), none of these new gcds is divisible by \(p\). Every new factor consequently has \(p\)-adic valuation zero. It follows that
\[
\nu_p(N(m+1))=\nu_p(N(m)).                                    \tag{9}
\]

Now consider the denominator. The case \(m=0\) is immediate: both \(D(0)\) and \(D(1)\) are \(1\). Assume henceforth that \(m>0\). Additivity of valuations and Legendre's formula give
\[
\nu_p(D(m+1))
=\sum_{k=1}^{m+1}k\sum_{i\ge1}
 \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor(m+1)/k\rfloor}{p^i}\right\rfloor,
                                                               \tag{10}
\]
whereas
\[
\nu_p(D(m))
=\sum_{k=1}^{m}k\sum_{i\ge1}
 \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/k\rfloor}{p^i}\right\rfloor.  \tag{11}
\]
The new term \(k=m+1\) in (10) is zero, because
\(\lfloor(m+1)/(m+1)\rfloor!=1!=1\), whose valuation is zero.
It remains to compare the terms with \(1\le k\le m\).

Fix such a \(k\) and an integer \(i\ge1\). By associativity of integer division,
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor(m+1)/k\rfloor}{p^i}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor\frac{m+1}{kp^i}\right\rfloor,
\]
and similarly
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/k\rfloor}{p^i}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor\frac{m}{kp^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
We use the elementary observation that for a positive integer \(Q\),
\[
Q\nmid m+1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\left\lfloor\frac{m+1}{Q}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor\frac mQ\right\rfloor.                           \tag{12}
\]
To see this, write \(m+1=Qh+r\) with \(0\le r<Q\). The hypothesis says
\(r>0\), so \(m=Qh+(r-1)\), and both quotients are \(h\).

Take \(Q=kp^i\). Because \(i\ge1\), \(p\mid kp^i\). If
\(kp^i\mid m+1\), then \(p\mid m+1\), contrary to the hypothesis. Hence (12) applies and yields
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor(m+1)/k\rfloor}{p^i}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/k\rfloor}{p^i}\right\rfloor.

after correcting the punctuation, this equality holds for every \(i\ge1\), so Legendre's formula implies
\[
\nu_p\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{m+1}{k}\right\rfloor!\right)
=
\nu_p\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac m k\right\rfloor!\right).
\]
Multiplying by \(k\), summing over \(1\le k\le m\), and recalling that the new \(k=m+1\) term is zero, we obtain
\[
\nu_p(D(m+1))=\nu_p(D(m)).                                    \tag{13}
\]

Combining (7), (9), and (13) proves the one-step assertion (8):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nu_p(a(m+1))
&=\nu_p(N(m+1))-\nu_p(D(m+1))\\
&=\nu_p(N(m))-\nu_p(D(m))\\
&=\nu_p(a(m)).
\end{aligned}
\]

We can now prove the conjecture. Let \(n\) be a positive integer, let \(p\) be prime, and let \(k\) satisfy \(0\le k<p\). We show by induction on \(k\) that
\[
\nu_p(a(np+k))=\nu_p(a(np)).                                  \tag{14}
\]
For \(k=0\), this is immediate. Suppose the assertion has been proved at an integer \(r\) with \(r+1<p\). To pass from \(np+r\) to \(np+r+1\), we claim that
\[
p\nmid np+r+1.                                                \tag{15}
\]
Indeed, if \(p\mid np+r+1\), then, since \(p\mid np\), subtraction would give \(p\mid r+1\). But \(1\le r+1<p\), and no positive multiple of \(p\) is strictly smaller than \(p\). This contradiction proves (15).

Apply the one-step assertion with \(m=np+r\). It gives
\[
\nu_p(a(np+r+1))=\nu_p(a(np+r)).
\]
The induction hypothesis identifies the right-hand side with
\(\nu_p(a(np))\), proving the next induction step. Thus (14) holds for every \(k<p\).

Equivalently,
\[
\nu_p(a(np))=\nu_p(a(np+1))=\cdots=\nu_p(a(np+p-1)),
\]
which is exactly the claimed constancy of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a(\cdot))\) on the indicated block.
